newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin warns Russia elite against power fight.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin warns Russia elite against power fight.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin told officials on Friday to stop fighting for power and made clear he planned to stay in office for his full four-year term.
"I want to remind the politicians -- Russia has made its choice for the next four years," Yeltsin, who is preparing for heart surgery, said in a radio address.
"There have been enough struggles for influence, fights for jobs, criticism and electioneering. It is time to work."

Yeltsin, 65, spoke clearly and sounded confident in the five-minute address, apparently recorded in the Barvika sanatorium where he is getting ready for a bypass operation to improve blood supply to his heart.
Russian and foreign doctors gave a green light to the surgery plans late last month and they say Yeltsin should be able to work normally again after the operation.
The president had two heart attacks last year and doctors say he may have had a third one before the second round of the Russian presidential election in July.
Yeltsin's announcement about the operation, now tentatively scheduled for the second half of November, led to a fight among top officials for control over Russia.

But under-the-carpet wrangling spilled out into the public last week, when Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov accused Yeltsin's national security adviser Alexander Lebed of plotting to seize power by force.
Yeltsin sacked Lebed, who had denied the accusations, and the gruff reserve paratroop general has not been charged with any wrongdoing.
Yeltsin, 65, said in the radio address that he was worried by recent public scandals involving top officials and would act firmly to prevent such rows in future.
"Such actions discredit the (state) powers, they are undermining citizens' confidence in the state," he said.

Yeltsin said Russia, which faced huge economic and social problems, badly needed a unified state power capable of concerted effort to make people's life better. He called on his political rivals to work together.
"An accord among powers should be accompanied by an accord among all our society," Yeltsin said. "We should stop dividing ourselved into red and white, into friends and foes."
"We should have only one criteria in assessing people -- their professionalism, their ability to work for the people's good and get results," he added.

It was Yeltsin's third radio address since he decided to start regular broadcasts to the nation. The first one dealt with general issues and the second one highlighted the problem of low tax revenues, setting up a special commission to decide how to rake in extra cash.
